summary: Defines how to advertise, in OSPF Router Information LSAs, the tunnel encapsulations that a router supports as a decapsulator. A router building a tunnel can then pick a type that the far end understands.

eli5.summary: Routers announce which kinds of tunnels they can receive, so senders choose one the receiver can open.

questions: how to advertise supported tunnel types in ospf
what is the ospf tunnel encapsulations tlv
how does ospf advertise tunnel types
what is ospf router information tlv type 13
what is the tunnel egress endpoint sub-tlv
subtitle: How an OSPF router tells its neighbors which tunnel types it can receive, so senders pick one the far end understands.

tldr.problem: A router that wants to send traffic through a tunnel must choose a tunnel type that the router at the far end can decapsulate, but it has no standard way to learn what the far end supports.
tldr.mechanism: The decapsulating router advertises a Tunnel Encapsulations TLV (type 13) in its OSPF Router Information Opaque LSA, listing each supported tunnel type and its parameters as sub-TLVs.
tldr.outcome: Encapsulating routers can combine this information with local policy, for example a color value, to pick a tunnel. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9013 is a Proposed Standard from April 2021 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the definition of how OSPF advertises tunnel encapsulations, and it builds on the BGP counterpart in RFC 9012.

sections.title: Why Advertise Tunnel Support
sections.content:
Networks use tunnels for many reasons. The RFC gives two examples: carrying IPv6 across IPv4 routers (or the reverse) as described in RFC 5565, and Remote Loop-Free Alternate repair tunnels as described in RFC 7490, where a tunnel runs between the Point of Local Repair and a selected PQ node.

Many tunnel types exist, and the tunnel encapsulator router must pick one that the tunnel decapsulator router supports. This document defines how the decapsulator lists its supported encapsulations in OSPF Router Information Link State Advertisements (LSAs). It covers both OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) and OSPFv3 (RFC 5340).
sections.eli5: If you want to mail a parcel to a friend, you should use a box they can open. This document lets routers say which boxes they can open.

sections.title: The Tunnel Encapsulations TLV
sections.content:
Routers advertise their supported tunnel types in a new TLV (a type, length, value item) of the OSPF Router Information (RI) Opaque LSA from RFC 7770. It is called the Tunnel Encapsulations TLV, its Type code is 13, its Length is variable, and it applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

The Value field holds one or more Tunnel Sub-TLVs. Each one describes one encapsulation format the router supports, plus the parameters for that tunnel type. The TLV MAY appear more than once in a single RI Opaque LSA. If it does, the Tunnel Sub-TLVs from all of the TLVs SHOULD be considered together. The scope of the advertisement depends on the application, but it SHOULD be domain wide.
sections.eli5: It is one labelled shelf on the router's sign. On the shelf are cards, one for each tunnel type the router can open.

sections.title: The Tunnel Sub-TLV
sections.content:
Each Tunnel Sub-TLV starts with a 2-octet Tunnel Type and a 2-octet Length, followed by zero or more Tunnel Parameter Sub-TLVs. Tunnel types are shared with the BGP extension in RFC 9012, so they come from the IANA registry called "BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute Tunnel Types". Unknown tunnel types are ignored on receipt.

Length counts the octets of the Tunnel Parameter Sub-TLVs field. If a Tunnel Sub-TLV is invalid, it MUST be ignored and skipped, but the other Tunnel Sub-TLVs MUST still be considered. One bad entry does not spoil the rest.
sections.eli5: Each card says which kind of tunnel it is and how long the card is, so a reader who does not know that tunnel can skip to the next card.

sections.title: Tunnel Parameter Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Inside a Tunnel Sub-TLV, each parameter has a 2-octet sub-type, a 2-octet length and a variable value. Several sub-types simply reuse definitions from other RFCs: Encapsulation (1), Protocol Type (2), DS Field (6) and UDP Destination Port (7) come from RFC 9012, and Load-Balancing Block (5) comes from RFC 5640.

Two are defined here. The Tunnel Egress Endpoint (type 3) carries the address of the router that will decapsulate the payload. It MUST appear once and only once per Tunnel Sub-TLV, holds a 2-octet Address Family and an address, and for IPv4 the Length MUST be 6, while for IPv6 it MUST be 18. IPv6 link-local addresses are not valid. The Color (type 4) is a 4-octet opaque unsigned integer, configured locally, that may appear zero or more times. Providers can use it in policy, and BGP routes carrying a Color Extended Community can express a wish to use a tunnel of the same color.

Any unknown sub-type MUST be ignored and skipped. A reserved value, or a value with bad syntax or semantics, makes that parameter invalid, and then its whole Tunnel Sub-TLV MUST be ignored while the others are still considered.
sections.eli5: The details on each card say things like where the tunnel ends and a color label chosen by the network owner. Cards with details a router cannot understand are skipped.

sections.title: How the Advertisement Is Used
sections.content:
Advertising a Tunnel Encapsulations Sub-TLV says that the advertising router supports a particular decapsulation, with the given parameters. Whether a tunnel is actually used depends on whether the encapsulator supports that type and on the encapsulator's own policy. The Color Sub-TLV may be an input to that policy. Some tunnel types may need an explicit tunnel setup protocol to run before data can flow.

One firm rule applies: a tunnel MUST NOT be used if there is no route toward the IP address in the Tunnel Egress Endpoint Sub-TLV, or if that route is not advertised in the same OSPF domain.
sections.eli5: The sign only says what a router can open. The sender still decides whether to use it, and it must not send parcels to an address outside the neighborhood.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA allocated value 13 for "Tunnel Encapsulations" in the "OSPF Router Information (RI) TLVs" registry. It also created the "OSPF Tunnel Parameter Sub-TLVs" registry. Values 1 to 34999 are allocated by Standards Action, and values 35000 to 65499 by First Come First Served. Values 65500 to 65534 are experimental, and 0 and 65535 are reserved.
sections.eli5: A central office keeps the official list of numbers for each kind of card, so two groups never use the same number for different things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security issues of the tunnel protocols themselves are inherited, and the softwire mesh framework (RFC 5565) covers them. If a third party could change the information used to build encapsulation headers or to choose a tunnel, user packets could be misrouted, misdelivered or dropped. The RFC argues that this is unlikely because an OSPF routing domain is usually a well-controlled network under one administration.

The rule in Section 6 also helps: since a tunnel to an address outside the OSPF domain is forbidden, someone who has taken over an OSPF router cannot use these advertisements to send traffic to outside destinations, for example for inspection.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could change the sign, parcels could go to the wrong place. But the neighborhood is usually locked, and parcels may not be sent outside it.

fields.name: Tunnel Type
fields.desc: Identifies the tunneling technology, using the BGP tunnel types registry.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total octets of the Tunnel Parameter Sub-TLVs field.

items.label: Tunnel Egress Endpoint
items.desc: Address of the decapsulating router; exactly one per Tunnel Sub-TLV.

items.label: Color
items.desc: Opaque 4-octet value used in local policy.
